title: The second drop
intro:
Mrs. Corazon Dizon, 68, has diabetes and high blood pressure. She dialyzes three times a week through a left arm fistula. She came in 3.8 kilograms above her dry weight of 52 kilograms, and the whole amount is being removed over four hours. She started at 152/86 mm Hg.

At hour 2:40 the nurse, Mr. Paolo Cruz, calls you to her chair. She is yawning, her calves are cramping, and she says she feels faint. Fluid removal is still running. He is waiting for your direction.

choices.text: Recline her, have fluid removal stopped, recheck the pressure, and count her pulse.
choices.feedback: These first steps return blood to the heart and stop the loss. Stopping fluid removal lets refilling from the tissues catch up. The blood pump keeps running, because nothing points to air, hemolysis, a reaction, or blood loss.

choices.text: Ask for a saline portion at once, before anything else.
choices.feedback: Fluid treats the result, not the cause, and it stays in a patient who passes little urine. With fluid removal still running, the machine keeps taking out what you put in.
choices.then: The saline runs in while fluid removal continues. Her pressure is 80/48 mm Hg. Mr. Cruz then reclines the chair and stops fluid removal.

choices.text: Halve the fluid removal rate so she still reaches her goal, and recheck the pressure in 15 minutes.
choices.feedback: A lower rate still removes fluid from a patient whose defenses have already failed. Fifteen minutes is too long to wait with a pressure in the 80s and symptoms.
choices.then: Five minutes later she is gray and nauseated, at 76/44 mm Hg. Mr. Cruz reclines the chair and stops fluid removal.

choices.text: Have the session ended now and the blood returned.
choices.feedback: A simple drop is not a reason to end the session, and you have not yet looked at her. Ending in a rush skips the steps that tell you whether this is simple or sinister. She also needs the rest of her treatment.
choices.then: Mr. Cruz hesitates and asks you to see her first. He reclines the chair and stops fluid removal while you examine her.

n2.scene: Lying back with fluid removal stopped, she says the faintness is easing. Her pressure is 98/60 mm Hg and her pulse is 90 and regular. The cramps are settling.

choices.text: Ask about chest pain and breathing, check the access and lines, and check glucose.
choices.feedback: This is the search for a dangerous cause. Pain or breathlessness points to the heart. A needle can slip out under a blanket. Low sugar mimics a pressure drop in a patient with diabetes.
choices.then: She denies chest pain and breathlessness. Both needles are secure and the lines are intact. Her glucose is 128 mg/dL.

choices.text: Ask for a capillary glucose and wait for the result.
choices.feedback: A glucose check is right in a patient with diabetes, but it is one item. You have not asked about chest pain or looked at the access and the lines.
choices.then: Her glucose is 128 mg/dL. You then ask about chest pain and uncover her arm. Nothing else is found.

choices.text: Her pressure is recovering, so restart fluid removal at the original rate to reach her goal on time.
choices.feedback: Do not restart at the old rate by reflex. The rate that caused the drop will cause it again. The remaining goal and time belong to the prescription and the attending nephrologist.
choices.then: Within minutes she yawns again and her pressure falls to 82/50 mm Hg. Fluid removal is stopped again. You then check her access, her symptoms, and her glucose (128 mg/dL).

n3.scene: Ten minutes later she is comfortable at 106/64 mm Hg. About 2.6 kilograms have been removed. Mr. Cruz asks what to do about the rest of the fluid goal.

choices.text: Call the attending with SBAR and ask how to continue.
choices.feedback: The episode is not finished until the nephrologist knows and the plan for the rest of the session is agreed. Her rate was about 18 mL per kg per hour, which is fast. That is part of your report.
choices.then: The attending nephrologist advises continuing without further fluid removal for now and reviewing her dry weight and salt intake at the next visit.

choices.text: Keep fluid removal off and plan to resume at half the rate in 20 minutes; tell the nephrologist at the end of the shift.
choices.feedback: Keeping fluid removal off is safe. But the new goal and rate are the nephrologist’s decision, and the call should come now, not at the end of the shift.
choices.then: You call. The attending nephrologist advises no further fluid removal for now.

choices.text: Ask Mr. Cruz to give a second saline portion to build a margin before restarting fluid removal.
choices.feedback: She has recovered, so more fluid is not needed. Giving fluid in order to remove it again adds to the load the session has to take off.
choices.then: You hold the saline and call the attending nephrologist, who advises no further fluid removal for now.

n4.scene: Twenty-five minutes later Mr. Cruz calls again. Mrs. Dizon is sweating and pressing her chest. “Mabigat,” she says: heavy. Her pressure is 78/46 mm Hg, her pulse is fast and irregular, and fluid removal has been off since hour 2:45.

choices.text: Emergency protocol: help, ECG, monitor, oxygen, and the attending at once.
choices.feedback: A second drop with chest pain and an abnormal pulse is not a simple drop, and fluid removal is no longer running to explain it. Diabetes can hide ischemia until late. Do not wait to see whether the pressure recovers.

choices.text: Give another saline portion, as the first drop responded to the first steps, and recheck in ten minutes.
choices.feedback: A patient who needs repeated fluid does not have a simple drop. Chest heaviness and an irregular, fast pulse are red flags. Every minute of waiting is a minute without an ECG.
choices.then: After the saline she is 80/50 mm Hg and still in pain. You call for help and get the ECG.

choices.text: Reassure her that this is the same cramping episode and keep fluid removal off.
choices.feedback: This anchors on the first diagnosis. The new features, chest heaviness, sweating, and a fast irregular pulse, point to a dangerous cause. A missed heart attack or rhythm problem can kill within minutes to hours.
choices.then: Mr. Cruz is worried and calls for help. The ECG is done ten minutes later than it could have been.

n5.scene: The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 130 per minute with new ST depression. The attending nephrologist advises ending the session and transferring her to the emergency department. The circuit is running normally: no alarms, and the blood in the lines looks normal.
n5.prompt: Is the blood in the circuit returned before transfer?

choices.text: Yes: the cause is in the patient and the circuit is sound.
choices.feedback: Returning the blood gives her back the volume in the circuit, which helps a patient with a low pressure. Blood is withheld only when the blood or the circuit may be the cause: air, hemolysis, a severe dialyzer reaction, or a clotted circuit.

choices.text: No. Clamp the lines and discard the circuit, since returning blood takes time and she needs to leave now.
choices.feedback: Withholding the blood is right when the circuit may be the cause. Here it is not, so discarding it takes away volume from a patient who is already hypotensive.

choices.text: Leave her connected and let the emergency team decide.
choices.feedback: The attending nephrologist has already decided to end the session. Leaving her connected delays the transfer. Returning the blood is part of ending the session safely in the unit.

end.title: Transfer
end.text: Her blood is returned and she leaves for the emergency department on a cardiac monitor with a nurse. You give an SBAR handover. In the record you write the times, the pressures and pulses, the steps and her response, the fluid given and removed, the ECG, the advice received, and her condition when she left.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • The first drop was simple. Hour three, a fast fluid removal rate (3.8 kg over 4 hours in a 52 kg patient is about 18 mL/kg/h), cramps, and a quick recovery all fit.
  • The second drop was not. It came with fluid removal off, with chest heaviness, sweating, and a fast irregular pulse. A patient who drops again after recovering, or who needs repeated fluid, needs a new look.
  • Stop and call. No recovery after first steps, a second drop, or any red flag means an immediate call to the attending nephrologist, while the protocol continues.
  • Return the blood when the cause is in the patient and the circuit is sound. Withhold it for air, hemolysis, a severe reaction, or a clotted circuit.

See the lesson parts The response, Simple or sinister, and the call card.
